summary.text: The Catalan recurrence implies that from index 2 onward successive reciprocals shrink by at least a factor of \(2/5\), so each leading term exceeds the whole subsequent tail; hence the interval sums lie in \((0,1)\) and are strictly ordered first by decreasing left endpoint and, for a fixed left endpoint, by increasing right endpoint. The sole exceptional interval sums to \(1\), whose fractional part is \(0\), so it cannot collide with the others.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}
\]
be the \(n\)-th Catalan number, and put
\[
b_n=\frac1{C_n}>0.
\]
For integers \(j\le k\), write
\[
S(j,k)=\sum_{i=j}^k b_i=\sum_{i=j}^k\frac1{C_i}.
\]
We prove that the fractional parts of the admissible sums \(S(j,k)\), where
\[
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k,
\]
are pairwise distinct.

First we establish the growth estimate for the Catalan numbers that drives the argument. From the defining formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{C_{n+1}}{C_n}
&=\frac{\binom{2n+2}{n+1}/(n+2)}{\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1)}\\
&=\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{(n+1)^2}\cdot\frac{n+1}{n+2}\\
&=\frac{2(2n+1)}{n+2}
 =\frac{4n+2}{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(n+2)C_{n+1}=(4n+2)C_n. \tag{1}
\]
Since \(C_0=1\), this recurrence also shows inductively that every \(C_n\) is positive. Taking reciprocals in (1) gives
\[
\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}=\frac{n+2}{4n+2}.
\]
If \(n\ge2\), then
\[
5(n+2)\le 2(4n+2),
\]
because this inequality is equivalent to \(6\le3n\). Therefore
\[
b_{n+1}\le \frac25 b_n\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{2}
\]

Iterating (2), for every \(j\ge2\) and every integer \(d\ge0\), we obtain
\[
b_{j+d}\le \left(\frac25\right)^d b_j. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the case \(d=0\) is equality, and if it holds for \(d\), then \(j+d\ge2\), so
\[
b_{j+d+1}\le\frac25b_{j+d}
\le\left(\frac25\right)^{d+1}b_j.
\]
In particular, \(b_n\) is nonincreasing for \(n\ge2\).

We next record a finite geometric-sum estimate. For \(j\ge2\) and \(d\ge0\), (3) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=j}^{j+d-1}b_i
&=\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}b_{j+r}\\
&\le b_j\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\left(\frac25\right)^r\\
&=\frac{1-(2/5)^d}{1-2/5}\,b_j\\
&=\left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^d\right)\frac53b_j. \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
(The sum is empty when \(d=0\), in which case the same formula holds.)

The crucial consequence is that every finite tail lying strictly after index \(j\) has sum smaller than the term at index \(j\): if \(j\ge2\) and \(k\ge j\), then
\[
\sum_{i=j+1}^k b_i<b_j. \tag{5}
\]
If \(k=j\), the left side is the empty sum \(0\), so (5) follows from \(b_j>0\). Suppose now that \(k\ge j+1\), and set \(d=k-j\). Applying (4) with initial index \(j+1\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=j+1}^k b_i
\le \left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^d\right)\frac53b_{j+1}.
\]
By (2), \(b_{j+1}\le(2/5)b_j\), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=j+1}^k b_i
&\le \left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^d\right)\frac53\cdot\frac25b_j\\
&=\left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^d\right)\frac23b_j\\
&\le\frac23b_j<b_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (5).

We now derive three properties of the interval sums.

First, for \(2\le j\le k\),
\[
0<S(j,k)<1. \tag{6}
\]
Positivity follows because the interval is nonempty and every \(b_i\) is positive. For the upper bound, split off the first term and use (5):
\[
S(j,k)=b_j+\sum_{i=j+1}^k b_i<2b_j.
\]
Since the \(b_n\) are nonincreasing from index \(2\) onward,
\[
b_j\le b_2.
\]
But \(C_2=\binom42/3=2\), so \(b_2=1/2\). Consequently
\[
S(j,k)<2b_j\le2b_2=1,
\]
which proves (6).

Second, an interval beginning later always has smaller sum, regardless of its ending point. More precisely, suppose
\[
2\le j_1\le k_1,\qquad 2\le j_2\le k_2,
\qquad j_1<j_2.
\]
Every index in \([j_2,k_2]\) is strictly greater than \(j_1\), so, using positivity of the terms,
\[
S(j_2,k_2)
\le \sum_{i=j_1+1}^{k_2}b_i.
\]
By (5), the right side is strictly less than \(b_{j_1}\). On the other hand, \(b_{j_1}\) is one of the positive summands of \(S(j_1,k_1)\), and hence
\[
b_{j_1}\le S(j_1,k_1).
\]
Thus
\[
S(j_2,k_2)<S(j_1,k_1). \tag{7}
\]

Third, if the starting index is fixed, extending the ending index strictly increases the sum. Namely, if
\[
2\le j\le k_1<k_2,
\]
then
\[
S(j,k_2)=S(j,k_1)+\sum_{i=k_1+1}^{k_2}b_i.
\]
The added interval is nonempty and all of its terms are positive, so
\[
S(j,k_1)<S(j,k_2). \tag{8}
\]

It follows at once from (7) and (8) that all sums \(S(j,k)\) with \(2\le j\le k\) are distinct. Indeed, compare two such pairs \((j_1,k_1)\) and \((j_2,k_2)\). If \(j_1<j_2\), (7) says the second sum is strictly smaller than the first. If \(j_2<j_1\), the reverse application of (7) says the first is strictly smaller. If \(j_1=j_2\), then unequal pairs must have \(k_1\ne k_2\), and (8), applied in the appropriate direction, distinguishes the sums.

It remains to connect this strict inequality statement to fractional parts and to handle the exceptional admissible pair. The index condition
\[
0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k
\]
has a simple dichotomy. Since \(0<\min\{2,k\}\), we have \(k\ge1\). If \(k=1\), then \(1=\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k=1\), so necessarily \((j,k)=(1,1)\). If \(k\ne1\), then \(k\ge2\), so \(\min\{2,k\}=2\), and therefore \(2\le j\le k\). Thus every admissible pair is either
\[
(1,1)
\]
or belongs to the ordinary range \(2\le j\le k\).

For the exceptional pair, \(C_1=\binom21/2=1\), and hence
\[
S(1,1)=\frac1{C_1}=1.
\]
Its fractional part is therefore \(0\).

For every other admissible pair, (6) says that \(S(j,k)\) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). The fractional part of a real number \(x\) in this open interval is \(x\) itself, since \(\lfloor x\rfloor=0\). Thus
\[
\{S(j,k)\}=S(j,k)\qquad(2\le j\le k), \tag{9}
\]
and this fractional part is strictly positive. In particular it cannot equal the fractional part \(0\) of \(S(1,1)\).

Finally, take any two distinct admissible pairs \((j_1,k_1)\) and \((j_2,k_2)\). If one is \((1,1)\), the other has \(2\le j\le k\), so their fractional parts are respectively \(0\) and a number strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). If neither is \((1,1)\), then both sums lie in \((0,1)\), so by (9) equality of their fractional parts would be equality of the sums themselves. But (7) distinguishes them when their starting indices differ, and (8) distinguishes them when their starting indices agree but their ending indices differ. Therefore their fractional parts cannot be equal.

Hence the rational numbers
\[
\sum_{i=j}^k\frac1{C_i},
\qquad 0<\min\{2,k\}\le j\le k,
\]
have pairwise distinct fractional parts.
